                                               PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                               §               BEFORE THE
 LARG LOAD INTERCONNECTION                             §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                         §                OF TEXAS

    THE STEERING COMMITTEE OF CITIES SERVED BY ONCOR AND TEXAS
   COALITION FOR AFFORDABLE POWER’S COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR
                  PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.194

         The Steering Committee of Cities Served by Oncor (OCSC) and Texas Coalition for

Affordable Power (TCAP) (collectively, Cities) submit these comments (Comments) to the Public

Utility of Commission of Texas (Commission) regarding proposed new 16 Tex. Admin. Code

(TAC) § 25.194 relating to large load interconnection standards. The Commission requested

interested persons to file comments by April 17, 2026.1 Therefore, these comments are timely

filed.

                                          I.     INTRODUCTION

         OCSC and TCAP are groups of over 170 municipalities and political subdivisions that, as

local governments, participate and have a unique interest in the energy market. In one capacity,

Cities are consumers that purchase electricity for various uses, including functions critical to the

health and safety of the Texans who live within their boundaries. These functions are provided

through public funds and, as stewards of these funds, Cities rely on just and reasonable energy

prices. Additionally, Cities participate in energy policy making to safeguard the health and safety

of their constituents. A reliable power grid ensures Cities’ citizens have access to critical functions

such as police, fire, ambulance, and emergency coordination. OCSC and TCAP, therefore, have

an interest in the large load interconnection standards at issue in this project.




         1
             Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC §25.194 (Mar. 12, 2026) (PFP).


                                                           1
                                   II.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       As requested, Cities have provided a one-page Executive Summary at the end of this

submission.

                                  III.    GENERAL COMMENTS

       Cities appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the Commission’s proposed new

16 TAC § 25.194 relating to the implementation of large load interconnection standards. As

explained below, Cities’ interest in this rulemaking is to assure that the private benefit of

interconnection and transmission upgrades are paid by the private parties that benefit from this

expansion. Cities as consumers, and the citizens and businesses located within their boundaries,

should be insulated from the costs of the interconnection of large loads and any risks of stranded

transmission assets associated with their interconnection efforts.

       In the adoption of Senate Bill (SB) 6, the Legislature articulated a dual responsibility that

the Commission must balance in its implementation of the legislation. Public Utility Regulatory

Act (PURA) § 37.0561(b) requires the Commission to “establish standards for interconnecting

large load customers in the ERCOT [Electric Reliability Council of Texas] power region in a

manner designed to support business development in this state while minimizing the potential for

stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.”2 The Legislature directed the

Commission to support business development while safeguarding consumers from stranded costs

and maintaining reliability. The Legislature went further in PURA § 35.004(c-1), instructing the

Commission to “ensure that a large load customer who is subject to the standards adopted under




       2
           Public Utility Regulatory Act, Tex. Util. Code § 37.0561(b) (PURA).


                                                        2
 Section 37.0561 contributes to the recovery of the interconnecting electric utility’s costs to

interconnect the large load to the utility’s system.”3

       The Legislature’s direction to the Commission to require that large loads contribute to their

interconnection costs is a significant shift in transmission cost allocation policy. Since the

beginning of electric restructuring in Texas, the Legislature and the Commission developed the

postage-stamp policy that equalized transmission costs for all consumers in ERCOT. That policy

was based on the recognition of network benefit, that transmission expansion benefited the entire

network, allowing consumers to source power from any competitive location in ERCOT to achieve

service at the lowest cost. This approach to transmission expansion cost recovery is at the heart

of the success of the ERCOT system during the restructuring era, in particular the ERCOT region’s

success in expanding its transmission network to serve consumers reliably and at lowest cost.

       In SB 6, the Legislature adopted a significant departure from the postage-stamp method.

The Legislature recognized that the expansion of transmission facilities to serve specifically these

large loads can no longer be justified as a network benefit but instead provides private benefit to

individual large loads. As such, the Legislature adopted a dual objective in SB 6, that the

legislation promote economic development in the State while assuring that large loads pay for the

private benefit of transmission expansions to serve them and protect Texas’ other consumers from

stranded costs and reliability degradation.

       The proliferation of large loads across Texas—in particular, the data centers under

discussion in ERCOT’s batch study process—raise questions of reliability and cost allocation. The

Commission’s task in adoption of the rule—and the related task of ERCOT in developing the batch

study framework—is to promote expansion of the data center industry, while creating a framework



       3
           PURA § 35.004(c-1).


                                                  3
 for private transmission funding for private benefit—all while ensuring reliability of the network

is maintained. The ever-expanding interconnection queue and the uncertainty now inherent in

ERCOT’s load forecast demonstrate the difficulty of striking that balance.

       As projected demand, which is largely due to data centers, rises in ERCOT, large load

interconnection standards are a vital piece of the overall large load regulation reform. Cities note,

however, that discussions around large loads as a whole are highly localized and involve various

pressing issues besides interconnection standards, including, but not limited to, the large load’s

suitability for a given location, land and water usage, and community impact.

       That being said, transmission costs are rising dramatically in Texas, with ERCOT

transmission projects in engineering, routing, licensing and construction totaling approximately

$32.631 billion as of February 1, 2026, and growing.4 Considering this total was $16.866 billion

only a year prior,5 Cities expect that total transmission costs will continue to climb, resulting in an

inevitable and large increase in their members’ electric bills and the bills of their citizens. To the

extent these volatile large loads are interconnected to the ERCOT grid, Cities urge the Commission

to carry out the intent of the Legislature by protecting consumers from stranded infrastructure costs

as well as any unnecessary cost increases.

       Cities offer specific comments related to the PFP below.

 A. Transparency and Flow of Financial Commitments

       Cities are particularly concerned with costs related to interconnecting large loads that may

not materialize and could then fall onto their citizens. Proposed new 16 TAC § 25.194 lays out

various financial commitments that large load customers must provide in order to lessen the risks

of expenses incurred by electric utilities and consumers related to projects that are not completed

as proposed.6 Specifically, the rule includes seven categories of fees and security requirements:

(1) a study fee paid by the large load customer for costs to conduct the interconnection study;7 (2)

financial security on a dollar per megawatt (MW) basis due at the time the intermediate agreement

is executed;8 (3) financial security for significant equipment or services as part of the intermediate

agreement;9 (4) a non-refundable interconnection fee;10 (5) financial security for significant

equipment or services as part of the interconnection agreement;11 (6) contribution in aid of

construction;12 and (7) financial security for system upgrades.13 However, the only fee categories

which appear to be non-refundable are (1), (4), and (6).14 Cities urge the Commission to ensure

that consumers are not negatively impacted by resulting cost increases and that these large loads

pay for the total of fees and security requirements to cover any and all costs of interconnection and

system upgrades needed to provide them service at their requested peak contracted demand or the

levels identified in ERCOT’s batch studies. This can be accomplished by keeping the level of

 financial security high enough to ensure only viable large load customers request to interconnect

and by better defining the financial commitments in the rule and the refund policies.

       To that end, Cities ask for more transparency in the proposed rule surrounding the various

fees and financial commitments, in particular the flow of funds among the fee categories. As

drafted, the alignment of the various fees is somewhat confusing and possibly overlapping. For

example, the proposed rule requires large load customers to post financial security for significant

equipment or service as part of both the intermediate and interconnection agreements.15 However,

both instances require the interconnecting Distribution Service Provider (DSP) or interconnecting

Transmission Service Provider (TSP) to apply any unused study fee that the large load paid under

the intermediate agreement to satisfy the financial security.16 It is unclear why the study fee in

particular is being used to offset the financial security for significant equipment or service.

       In addition, the proposed financial security that a large load customer must post on a dollar

per MW basis is insufficiently clear as drafted.17 A large load customer must post $50,000 per

MW of requested peak demand to the interconnecting DSP or TSP as part of the intermediate

agreement.18 A large load customer must also pay a non-refundable interconnection fee in the

amount of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand as part of the interconnection agreement.19

As drafted, the proposed rule is unclear as to whether the $50,000 per MW posted as part of the

intermediate agreement offsets the non-refundable interconnection fee. Moreover, besides what

is prescribed in proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(g), the rule does not detail the extent to which a large

 load customer will be refunded for financial security posted as part of the intermediate agreement

if ERCOT does not award that customer the full amount of its requested peak demand and that

customer thus decides to withdraw its requested peak demand. Cities are concerned that large load

customers may withdraw projects if they are not awarded their requested peak demand and expect

regular disputes to occur between the large loads and ERCOT as to the amount refunded if this

occurs. Cities urge the Commission to consider all stakeholder comments addressing the financial

commitments in the proposed rule to ensure maximum transparency.

B. Application of Financial Commitments

         Another area of uncertainty in the proposed rule relates to how the financial commitments

are applied. In some instances, financial security would be used to prefund utility expenses for

interconnecting the large load customer,20 whereas in others it would be applied to offset the

interconnecting TSP’s rate base.21 This particular distinction between when financial security

should be applied to prefund utility expenses versus when it should be used to offset rate base

further highlights that the flow of funds among the fee categories is not clearly defined and difficult

to trace. A clearer, more straightforward financial structure will help ensure that ratepayers avoid

paying costs which are the responsibility of large load customers. The Commission should fully

translate the intent of each financial commitment so that parties know exactly what they are

responsible for and where the fees are going. Along with completely defining each financial

commitment in the proposed rule to remove any discrepancies, Cities recommend the Commission

 include all categories of fees under one subsection so that they are readily available and easier to

review.

          Cities recommend a modification to the proposal requiring the interconnecting TSP to

offset its rate base with funds provided by large loads. The proposed rule includes multiple areas

where the interconnecting TSP must offset its rate base with amounts collected from large loads.22

For example, proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7) states that the interconnecting TSP must apply the

non-refundable interconnection fee paid by the large load customer as an offset to its rate base in

the earlier of that interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate proceeding or comprehensive rate

proceeding.23 Considering the ERCOT system as a whole, where the benefits from system

upgrades provide benefits across the network, all ratepayers currently pay for transmission

upgrades and investment through the postage-stamp method.24                   A reduction to a specific

interconnecting TSP’s rate base in this instance would benefit customers in the interconnecting

TSP’s service area without recognizing the benefit to the network, as is the basis for the original

postage-stamp allocation policy. These funds provided by large load customers should offset the

overall transmission cost of service in ERCOT rather than an individual TSP’s rate base. Cities

acknowledge that transmission cost recovery is currently being addressed in Project No. 58484

and there may be overlap between issues addressed in that rulemaking and the one at hand.25 The

Commission should take this opportunity to revise the applicable provisions in the proposed rule

 so that financial security is fairly applied to all TSPs across ERCOT – not just the interconnecting

TSP.

                                    V.     CONCLUSION

       Cities appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Commission’s rulemaking regarding

large load interconnection standards. Cities look forward to future work sessions, discussions, and

opportunities for stakeholder engagement regarding large load interconnection standards and

appreciate the opportunity to submit these Comments to the Commission.

      THE STEERING COMMITTEE OF CITIES SERVED BY ONCOR AND TEXAS
       COALITION FOR AFFORDABLE POWER’S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       Cities as consumers, and the citizens and businesses located within their boundaries, should

        be insulated from the costs of the interconnection of large loads and any risks of stranded

        transmission assets associated with their interconnection efforts.

       Large load customers should pay for the entirety of the fees and security requirements laid

        out in the proposed rule to cover any and all costs of interconnection and system upgrades

        needed to provide them service since expansion of transmission facilities to serve these

        large loads provides a private benefit.

        o The level of financial security should be high enough to ensure only viable large load

            customers request to interconnect, and the financial commitments and refund policies

            in the rule should be more clearly defined to remove any discrepancies.

       Cities ask for more transparency in the proposed rule surrounding the various fees and

        financial commitments.

        o The alignment of the various fees and financial commitments in the proposed rule is

            somewhat confusing and possibly overlapping.

       The Commission should fully translate the intent of each financial commitment so that

        parties know exactly what they are responsible for and where the fees are going.

        o All categories of fees should be included under one subsection so that they are readily

            available and easier to review.

       Provisions in the proposed rule requiring the interconnecting Transmission Service

        Provider to offset its rate base with funds provided by large loads should be modified to

        require an offset to the overall transmission cost of service in ERCOT instead.

     THE STEERING COMMITTEE OF CITIES SERVED BY ONCOR AND TEXAS
       COALITION FOR AFFORDABLE POWER'S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

•       Cities as consumers, and the citizens and businesses located within their boundaries, should

        be insulated from the costs of the interconnection of large loads and any risks of stranded

        transmission assets associated with their interconnection efforts.

•       Large load customers should pay for the entirety of the fees and security requirements laid

        out in the proposed rule to cover any and all costs of interconnection and system upgrades

        needed to provide them service since expansion of transmission facilities to serve these
        large loads provides a private benefit.

        o   The level of financial security should be high enough to ensure only viable large load

            customers request to interconnect, and the financial commitments and refund policies

            in the rule should be more clearly defined to remove any discrepancies.

•       Cities ask for more transparency in the proposed rule surrounding the various fees and

        financial commitments.

        o   The alignment of the various fees and financial commitments in the proposed rule is

             somewhat confusing and possibly overlapping.

•       The Commission should fully translate the intent of each financial commitment so that

        parties know exactly what they are responsible for and where the fees are going.

        o   All categories of fees should be included under one subsection so that they are readily

            available and easier to review.

•       Provisions in the proposed rule requiring the interconnecting Transmission Service

        Provider to offset its rate base with funds provided by large loads should be modified to

        require an offset to the overall transmission cost of service in ERCOT instead.
